query: W is attractive for plasma-facing divertor components because of its high melting point, thermal resistance, low sputtering yield, and low tritium retention, but its relatively high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature limits use. CuCrZr provides favorable thermal conductivity as a heat sink but has a narrow operating-temperature range and is susceptible to irradiation embrittlement, requiring an intermediate layer that transfers heat efficiently while keeping both materials within suitable temperature ranges. Earlier HEA studies reported elevated-temperature strength retention in MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW, thermal stability in Mo6.6Nb6Ni80Ta1.4Ti6, and favorable combinations of strength and ductility in NbTaTiV, HfNbTaTiZr, and TiVNbTa. Nevertheless, HEA performance can involve tradeoffs among strength, ductility, thermal stability, and phase constitution. TiVNbTa in a single-phase BCC dendritic state combines about 800 MPa yield strength with approximately 40% strain, but its reported yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K are only 330 and 423 MPa, respectively, at 30% strain. Under the constraints of efficient W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer, high-temperature mechanical stability, and compatibility with the limited operating ranges of both adjoining materials, what single intervention could improve the TiVNbTa intermediate material? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted change relative to the reported TiVNbTa baseline, temperature and loading boundaries, supporting evidence from the prior HEA results, and a controlled experiment that would falsify both the performance prediction and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (approximately 2–5 at%) of chromium to the TiVNbTa alloy will induce the formation of a controlled dispersion of nanoscale, thermally stable, coherent Cr-rich intermetallic precipitates that bolster high-temperature yield strength while maintaining the matrix’s thermal conductivity for efficient W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase BCC dendritic TiVNbTa alloy that shows high strength and ductility at room temperature (≈800 MPa yield, ~40% strain) but reduced yield (≈330 MPa) and compressive strength (≈423 MPa) at around 1273 K.
generation.intervention: Alloying with a minor addition of chromium (≈2–5 at%) into the TiVNbTa formulation.
generation.conditions: Operational conditions pertinent to plasma‐facing divertor components, specifically high temperatures near 1273 K and mechanical loading representative of service conditions, while ensuring compatibility with the adjacent W and CuCrZr materials.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of finely dispersed, coherent Cr-rich intermetallic precipitates within the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The Cr addition is expected to promote a controlled precipitation process during appropriate heat treatments or in-service exposure. These nanoscale precipitates will impede dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding at elevated temperatures (precipitation strengthening), thereby improving the high-temperature mechanical stability, all while preserving the overall BCC matrix structure that supports high thermal conductivity necessary for efficient heat transfer between W and CuCrZr.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline TiVNbTa alloy, the Cr-modified alloy should display a significant improvement (on the order of roughly 30–50% increase) in high-temperature yield strength with retained ductility and thermal conductivity within the operating constraints.
generation.baseline: TiVNbTa in a single-phase BCC state with reported yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K of approximately 330 MPa and 423 MPa, respectively.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected when the Cr content is kept low (around 2–5 at%) to avoid formation of excessive brittle intermetallic phases that could compromise ductility or thermal transport. The improvement is anticipated under high-temperature mechanical loading conditions (near 1273 K), with performance remaining acceptable within the temperature limits imposed by the adjoining W and CuCrZr components.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the strength improvement and the stability of the precipitates depend on the precise Cr content and processing history. There is also some uncertainty regarding potential minor impacts on ductility or thermal conductivity that must be experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of TiVNbTa alloys with 0, 2, 3, and 5 at% Cr additions under identical processing conditions, followed by a controlled heat treatment designed to facilitate precipitation. Subject the samples to high-temperature tensile testing (at ~1273 K) and use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to characterize the microstructure and precipitate formation.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength and compressive strength
Microstructural parameters (precipitate size, distribution, phase identification)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-alloyed specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant (≥10%) improvement in high-temperature yield strength compared to the baseline or if the introduced Cr leads to formation of deleterious coarse or brittle phases that significantly reduce ductility or thermal conductivity, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In the last few decades, the development of nickel-based superalloys has allowed a steady increase in operating temperatures of jet turbine engines, which leads to enhanced engine performance and efficiency. However, nowadays the engine operating temperatures have reached around 80% of the melting points of the materials, [1] i.e. , almost reaching the upper limit of usability, making it impossible to further increase the operating temperature. Thus, it is urgently needed to develop new materials that can withstand higher operating temperatures to achieve better performance, higher engine efficiency, and lower greenhouse gas emissions.

Among various potential candidates, such as ceramics, [3] intermetallic compounds, [6] and refractory metals, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [8] have drawn considerable attention in the past decade because of their very encouraging properties, for instance, high melting points, superior mechanical properties at both room temperature and elevated temperatures, [13] which makes RHEAs of great interest for high-temperature application. One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ].
